questions.q: Why is inference often latency-bound while training is throughput-bound?
options: Inference always uses more GPUs than training
Training only measures aggregate progress through data with no single example waiting on a response, while inference often has a real user waiting right now for tokens to appear
Inference never uses batching, so it is always slower
Training and inference actually have identical performance profiles
questions.explain: Training optimizes for getting through as much data as possible per GPU-hour, with no one waiting on a single example. Interactive inference has a user waiting on a response right now, which makes latency, not just throughput, a first-class concern.

questions.q: What distinguishes the prefill phase from the decode phase when serving an autoregressive LLM?
options: Prefill and decode are identical; the terms are interchangeable
Prefill processes the full prompt in one compute-bound pass, while decode generates one token at a time and is memory-bandwidth-bound because of KV cache lookups
Decode happens before prefill in every request
Prefill only occurs when fine-tuning a model, never during inference
questions.explain: Prefill is a single forward pass over the whole prompt, which is compute-bound. Decode generates tokens one at a time, attending back over the KV cache, which is memory-bandwidth-bound rather than compute-bound.

questions.q: Which training-time architecture choice directly reduces KV cache size at serving time?
options: Increasing the vocabulary size
Using grouped-query attention (GQA) or multi-query attention (MQA) instead of plain multi-head attention (MHA)
Increasing the maximum supported context length
Switching from bf16 to fp32 during pretraining
questions.explain: GQA and MQA reduce the number of distinct key/value projections compared to full multi-head attention, directly shrinking the KV cache that must be stored per request at serving time.

questions.q: What does time-to-first-token (TTFT) primarily measure, and what phase dominates it?
options: The total cost of training the model; it has nothing to do with inference
The latency from request arrival until the first generated token appears, dominated by the prefill phase
The time it takes to load the model weights onto disk
The average latency per output token, dominated by the decode phase
questions.explain: TTFT is the latency from when a request arrives until the first output token is produced, and because that requires processing the full prompt first, it is dominated by the compute-bound prefill phase.

questions.q: Why can a model that trains efficiently still decode slowly in production?
options: Because training and decode are mathematically identical operations, so efficiency always transfers
Because training never exercises the one-token-at-a-time decode path at all -- it processes full sequences in parallel with teacher-forcing, so decode performance is untested by training throughput
Because decode speed depends only on the number of GPUs used during pretraining
Because efficient training always implies efficient decoding by definition
questions.explain: Training sees full sequences in parallel via teacher-forcing and never performs the sequential, memory-bandwidth-bound decode step that inference requires, so training throughput says nothing about decode latency.
